CausalChain: MCM5 upregulation -> Elevated replication stress (specifically beyond canonical MCM-driven replication) -> Preferential activation of the BIR pathway via RAD52 (modulated by epigenetic influences such as KMT5C) -> Aberrant double-strand break repair -> Genomic instability -> Enhanced tumor aggressiveness (metastasis and angiogenesis)
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in liver neoplasms, overexpression of MCM5 uniquely exacerbates replication stress beyond what is induced by classical MCM-driven replication (e.g., via MCM7). This excess replication stress triggers a preferential activation of the break-induced replication (BIR) pathway through enhanced interaction with RAD52. Epigenetic modulators like KMT5C may further bias the DNA repair landscape by promoting repair via error-prone BIR rather than high-fidelity homologous recombination. The resultant aberrant repair leads to genomic instability, fueling tumor aggressiveness manifested by increased metastasis and angiogenesis. This hypothesis not only refines the original model—which broadly linked MCM5 overexpression to tumor progression via a RAD52-mediated BIR mechanism—but also incorporates contemporary evidence highlighting alternative replication proteins and epigenetic factors. Modern technological approaches, including CRISPR-based functional genomics, single-cell proteomics, and live-cell imaging of DNA repair processes, will be instrumental in validating and dissecting the specificity and functional significance of the MCM5-RAD52 axis in liver cancer progression.
Abstract: In this study, we propose that a distinct subset of liver neoplasms exhibits a unique interaction between MCM5 overexpression and the DNA repair machinery, leading to enhanced genomic instability and tumor aggressiveness. While overexpression of MCM family members (e.g., MCM7) has been associated with robust replication initiation and cell proliferation via canonical pathways such as PI3K/AKT signaling, we hypothesize that MCM5, when aberrantly upregulated, imparts an additional, context-specific replication stress that preferentially activates the break-induced replication (BIR) pathway. This activation is mediated by its interaction with RAD52, an event potentially modulated by epigenetic factors such as KMT5C that influence repair pathway choice. We suggest that under conditions of elevated replication stress, the MCM5-RAD52 axis diverts repair processes toward error-prone BIR, resulting in abnormal double-strand break repair, genomic instability, increased metastatic potential, and heightened angiogenesis. Leveraging contemporary technologies such as CRISPR-based genetic screens, single-cell proteomic analyses, and real-time imaging of repair dynamics, our hypothesis aims to delineate the mechanistic nuances of this pathway and to identify novel therapeutic interventions that specifically target the MCM5-RAD52 interaction in liver cancer.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis centered on MCM5 overexpression inducing replication stress that activates the BIR pathway via RAD52, leading to genomic instability and tumor aggressiveness. The refined hypothesis retains these critical causal steps but introduces greater specificity by differentiating the role of MCM5 from other MCM family members (e.g., MCM7, which governs canonical replication initiation and PI3K/AKT signaling). It also acknowledges the influence of epigenetic regulators (such as KMT5C) on repair pathway choice. By integrating advanced technologies such as CRISPR screens, single-cell proteomic analysis, and real-time imaging, the new hypothesis not only addresses the mechanistic gaps identified in the original but also enhances its practical implementations for therapeutic targeting.
